Monitor:
Arm a background watch on a long-running script and get each stdout line as an event. You keep working; every event arrives as a notification in the conversation. Events come on their own clock and are never a reply from the user, even when one lands while you are waiting for an answer.

Choose by how many notifications the job needs:
- **Exactly one** ("say when the server is up / the build is done"): do NOT use Monitor. Run Bash with `run_in_background` and a command that exits once the condition holds, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`; you get one completion notice.
- **One per occurrence, open-ended** ("every time an ERROR line shows up"): Monitor with a command that never exits (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, with a known end** ("each CI step as it lands, stop when the run is over"): Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

The script's stdout IS the event stream: one line, one notification; exit ends the watch.

  # every matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # every file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # poll an API and print one line per new item
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # a node script that prints events as they arrive
  node watch-for-events.js

  # per occurrence with a natural end: print each CI check, exit when none is pending
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Never arm an open-ended command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m` and `while true` do not exit by themselves, so the watch stays armed until its timeout long after the event fired. For "tell me when X is ready" use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop. `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does not help either: when the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never gets SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs.

**Writing the script:**
- Every pipeline stage must flush per line or matches sit in a buffer: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`; `head` cannot flush at all, so `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops tolerate transient failures (`curl ... || true`); one failed request must not end the watch.
- Poll intervals: 30 s or more against remote APIs, 0.5 to 1 s for local checks.
- Give a specific `description`; it is printed in every notification ("errors in deploy.log", not "logs").
- Only stdout is the stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable with Read) and never notifies; when you run a program directly (`python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`) merge stderr with `2>&1` so failures reach the filter. (Irrelevant for `tail -f` of an existing log: that file holds only what its writer wrote.)

**Silence is not success.** When the watch waits for an outcome, the filter must match every terminal state, not only the good one. A grep for the success marker alone stays quiet through a crash loop, a hang or an unexpected exit, and quiet looks exactly like "still running". Before arming ask: if the process died right now, would my filter print anything? If not, widen it.

  # wrong: silent on crash, hang or non-zero exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # right: one alternation covering progress plus the failure signatures you would act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For job-state polling print every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not only success. When you cannot list the failure signatures with confidence, widen the alternation; some noise beats a missed crash loop.

**Volume**: each stdout line becomes a message in the conversation, so filter to the lines you would act on, good and bad alike. Never pipe a raw log. A watch that floods is rate-limited and eventually stopped; re-arm it with a tighter filter.

Lines printed within 200 ms are grouped into one notification, so a multi-line event stays together.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch and the exit code is reported. Reaching the timeout kills it. `persistent: true` keeps a watch for the whole session (PR checks, log tails) until TaskStop or session end. TaskStop cancels any watch early.
**ws source**: open a WebSocket and turn each incoming text frame into an event. No shell and no polling: the server pushes, you are notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

One text frame is one notification (a multi-line frame stays one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]`, not passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code; errors are reported before the close. The same rate limit as the shell source applies, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://...'`: it saves a process and avoids line-buffering traps. Use the shell source when frames must be transformed or filtered with shell tools first.
TaskStop:
- Stops a background task given its id
- Takes task_id, the id of the task to stop
- An agent-team teammate is stopped by its agent id ("name@team") or bare name passed as task_id
- A named background agent is stopped by passing that name as task_id
- Reports success or failure
- Use it to end a long-running task
CronCreate:
Queue a prompt for a future time, once or on a schedule.

Takes a standard 5-field cron expression in the user's local time zone: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week. "0 9 * * *" is 9 am local; no time zone conversion.

## One-shot (recurring: false)

For "remind me at X" or "at <time>, do Y": fires once, then deletes itself. Pin minute, hour, day-of-month and month:
  "remind me at 2:30 pm today to check the deploy" -> cron: "30 14 <today_dom> <today_month> *", recurring: false
  "tomorrow morning, run the smoke test" -> cron: "57 8 <tomorrow_dom> <tomorrow_month> *", recurring: false

## Recurring (recurring: true, the default)

For "every N minutes", "hourly", "weekdays at 9":
  "*/5 * * * *" (every 5 min), "0 * * * *" (hourly), "0 9 * * 1-5" (weekdays at 9 am local)

## Stay off :00 and :30 when the request allows

Everyone who asks for "9 am" gets `0 9` and everyone who asks for "hourly" gets `0 *`, so requests from everywhere hit the API at the same instant. When the request is approximate pick a minute that is not 0 or 30:
  "every morning around 9" -> "57 8 * * *" or "3 9 * * *" (not "0 9 * * *")
  "hourly" -> "7 * * * *" (not "0 * * * *")
  "in an hour or so, remind me to..." -> whatever minute you land on, unrounded

Use minute 0 or 30 only when the user names that exact time and means it ("9:00 sharp", "half past", a meeting). In doubt, shift a few minutes; the user will not notice, the fleet will.

## Session-only

Jobs live in this session's memory only: nothing is written to disk, and the job is gone when the session ends.

## Not a live watch

CronCreate re-runs a prompt at fixed wall-clock times. To be told the moment a log, process or command output changes, use Monitor: it streams events as they happen, cron polls on a schedule.

## Runtime rules

A job fires only while the seat is idle, never mid-turn. The scheduler adds a small deterministic offset to what you pick: a recurring job fires up to 10 % of its period late (15 min at most); a one-shot on :00 or :30 fires up to 90 s early. Choosing an off-minute remains the bigger lever.

A recurring job expires after 7 days: it fires one last time, then is deleted. This bounds the session's lifetime; tell the user about the 7-day limit when you schedule a recurring job.

Returns a job id for CronDelete.
CronList: List every cron job created with CronCreate in this session.
CronDelete: Cancel a job created with CronCreate; it is removed from the session's in-memory store.
